title: Basa-Jauna and the Three Brothers
subtitle: A wild-man household in a Basque story

learningObjectives.text: What does the youngest brother see from the tree?
Who warns the brothers about the Basa-Jaun?

wildman.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
wildman.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
wildman.locator: BASA-JAUNA, THE WILD MAN.; BASA-JAUNA, THE WILD MAN., normalized characters 1091-1635
wildman.excerpt: the three brothers set out together. At eight o'clock in the evening they come to a grand castle, and they knock at the door, and the Basa-Andre (wild woman) comes to answer. She asks: "Who is there?" And they reply, "It is we who are here." "What do you want, young children? Where are you going to at this time of night?" "We ask and beg of you to give us shelter for to-night; we will be satisfied with a corner of the floor, poor wretches as we are." "I have my husband, the Basa-Jaun, and if he catches you he will eat you; that's certain.
wildman.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: A trail of smoke
narrativeBlocks.body: Three brothers travel through a forest at night. The youngest sees a thin column of smoke in the distance and leads them toward a castle.

narrativeBlocks.title: A warning at the castle
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Webster's English collection; whitespace normalized): “the three brothers set out together. At eight o'clock in the evening they come to a grand castle, and they knock at the door, and the Basa-Andre (wild woman) comes to answer. She asks: "Who is there?" And they reply, "It is we who are here." "What do you want, young children? Where are you going to at this time of night?" "We ask and beg of you to give us shelter for to-night; we will be satisfied with a corner of the floor, poor wretches as we are." "I have my husband, the Basa-Jaun, and if he catches you he will eat you; that's certain.”

narrativeBlocks.title: The Basa-Andre opens the door
narrativeBlocks.body: The brothers ask for shelter. The Basa-Andre warns them that her husband, the Basa-Jaun, may eat them, but lets them in.

narrativeBlocks.title: Name the collection's variant
narrativeBlocks.body: Basa-Jauna and Basa-Andre appear in Webster's collection of Labourd stories. Preserve these names and this written version rather than treating them as the same figure in every local account.

narrativeBlocks.title: Hospitality exists beside danger
narrativeBlocks.body: The story begins with shelter offered in a household that the visitors have reason to fear.
